Good afternoon, Adrian. Rachel Wong here. We have our arranged portfolio review and dealing discussion. Are you somewhere you can speak comfortably, and have you been able to bring your notes with you?

Good afternoon, Rachel. Yes, I'm at home in the study. I've put the notes on the desk rather than trying to do this from my phone. That was a mistake on a previous call; I spent more time looking for the right document than actually talking. There's nothing pressing immediately after this, so we can have a proper conversation.

That sounds practical. Before we get into the review, may I take your identification details and date of birth for the call? Then we can leave the administrative opening behind us and give the discussion our attention.

My FIN is F five triple nine two four three L. My date of birth is the twenty-fifth of October nineteen eighty-four.

Thank you, Adrian. How would you like to use the discussion before we come to the dealing part? We can leave space for the changes in your working life as well as the practical arrangements for keeping in touch.

The working-life changes are probably the best place to start. On paper, I've stepped back from running the consulting business. In practice, people still remember that I used to be available for everything, so the boundary is taking a while to become real. I'm not complaining; it's rather flattering that people still want my opinion. But there is a difference between being asked for a view and quietly becoming responsible for the whole problem again. I'm learning to recognise when that distinction has disappeared.

Has the advisory role acquired a regular structure yet, or are you still finding out what the business needs from you? It would be useful to know how settled your availability is when we arrange our own conversations.

It's becoming more structured. The management team sends me material in advance now, which helps enormously. Previously someone would telephone and begin with, 'This will only take a moment,' and I would discover that we were discussing an entire staffing issue. Now I can read the background, give a considered response, and leave the decision with the person who actually owns it. I still enjoy the difficult questions. What I don't miss is being the person who has to remember every loose end after the meeting finishes.

For our arrangements, we can distinguish a planned review from an administrative query rather than treating every contact as a full discussion. That should also make the purpose of a call clearer when you see it in your diary.

That would be helpful. I don't want to create an elaborate system, but a clear purpose makes a difference. I'm trying to do the same with the business. If someone sends a meeting invitation with nothing except 'catch-up' in the subject line, I now ask what they want to discuss. It isn't an attempt to be difficult. I just find that a little preparation makes the conversation much better, and usually shorter. Today is different because I've deliberately left room to talk things through.

Your objective is to reduce the overlap between your technology investments and your business interests, giving you greater financial flexibility as you step back from the business.

I've brought the relevant holding notes, although they're mixed in with some older review pages. Let me keep those together while we talk. The personal adjustment has been interesting too. When I was running the business, my calendar made most decisions for me. Now an empty afternoon is actually mine to use, and I sometimes catch myself treating that as an administrative error. My family finds that rather amusing. They seem to have adapted to my supposedly quieter life more quickly than I have.

It sounds as though your diary is still finding its new shape. From the bank's perspective, it would help to know whether you prefer appointments to remain firmly scheduled, even when your day has more flexibility.

Definitely scheduled. Flexibility doesn't mean I want to be interrupted at random. I enjoy being able to decide that I'll spend a morning reading, or go out without wondering whether I've forgotten a meeting. A proper appointment lets me prepare and then put the subject away afterwards. The strange part is that I used to think spontaneity would be the great reward of stepping back. What I've actually appreciated is being able to choose my commitments rather than simply having fewer of them.

We can keep that distinction in mind for future contact. Are there still occasions when business commitments arise without much notice, or has the handover reduced those interruptions?

There are occasional interruptions, particularly when an old client asks to speak to me personally. I usually introduce the current lead and then step out, but some relationships need a little care. I built those relationships over a long period, so I don't want the handover to feel abrupt. At the same time, I don't want to stand behind the new team correcting their language. They need room to sound like themselves. That has probably been the hardest habit to break: allowing a perfectly good answer to be different from the answer I would have given.

That gives me a clearer picture of your availability. When something administrative needs attention, would a secure message generally be easier than an unscheduled telephone call?

Yes, provided the message says what it concerns. A vague request to call back can sit in my mind all afternoon, even if it's only about a document. If it's routine administration, I would rather see that immediately and deal with it when I'm at my desk. For a planned conversation, a calendar invitation is much better. I'm still perfectly happy to speak on the telephone; I just no longer carry it around as though I were on duty.

A clear subject and a concise description are sensible preferences to record. We should still keep confidential material within the appropriate bank channels, but the purpose of a message need not be mysterious. Have you had an opportunity to use some of the new flexibility for travel?

Yes, and I've discovered that I prefer a different sort of trip now. Business travel trained me to judge a place by how easily I could get from the airport to a meeting. Recently I stayed somewhere quiet enough that I could hear people opening the shutters in the morning. There was no great itinerary. I walked into town, found somewhere for coffee, and spent far longer than expected looking at a little public library. It was a pleasant shock to realise there was nowhere else I was supposed to be.

Was it the quieter setting that appealed most, or having the freedom to stay longer when something caught your attention?

The freedom, I think, although the setting helped. When you're travelling for work, every spare hour becomes a slot you feel obliged to use efficiently. I used to fit a museum between meetings and then remember almost nothing about it. This time I went back to the same square because I liked watching how it changed during the day. My family initially thought I must have run out of ideas. Eventually they realised that returning somewhere could be the point rather than evidence that the planning had failed.

Were you travelling together throughout, or did everyone have room to follow their own interests? That can make a difference to how available you want to be for calls while away.

We travelled together, but we didn't insist on doing everything together. That was much more agreeable than trying to achieve consensus over every museum or lunch. Someone might want a long walk while someone else wanted to read. We met again later with something to tell each other. I also stopped checking business messages over breakfast. Nothing dramatic happened as a result, which was useful evidence that the world could manage without an immediate response from me.

For bank appointments during travel, would you prefer to leave them until you're home, unless there is a particular administrative reason to speak sooner?

For routine reviews, yes. I don't enjoy discussing private matters from a hotel corridor or wondering who can hear me through a connecting door. If something needs attention, a message asking me to arrange a suitable time is fine. I can find a quiet place and call properly. What I want to avoid is having a review pencilled in while I'm supposedly at leisure and then spending the morning looking for somewhere with a reliable connection.

We can ask about travel when arranging a review rather than assuming your usual routine applies. You mentioned the library that caught your attention. Was that mainly an architectural interest, or were you drawn in by what was happening inside?

Initially the building. It had a very restrained entrance, almost too modest to notice, and then the interior opened into a lovely reading room. But I stayed because people were using it so naturally. There were schoolchildren at a table, an older man reading the papers, someone asking a librarian for help. I like architecture that has a life beyond the photograph. A dramatic building can be enjoyable to look at, but I'm increasingly interested in whether people seem comfortable spending time there.

Do you tend to seek those places out in advance, or discover them while walking? I'm asking partly because it sounds as though you now leave more of a trip unplanned.

A mixture. I read enough beforehand to know what I might enjoy, but I don't want the research to become an obligation. My old habit was to make a list and then feel vaguely dissatisfied if anything remained unticked. Now I keep a few possibilities and allow the weather or my mood to decide. The library wasn't on the list. Neither was a small exhibition in a former workshop, which turned out to be much more memorable than a famous place we had booked well ahead.

That sounds like a useful distinction between preparation and a timetable. When you return from a trip, do you generally want some space before resuming appointments, or are you comfortable going straight back into your diary?

Some space is preferable. I used to arrive home and schedule meetings immediately, as if unpacking were something that happened automatically around the edges. These days I'd rather settle in, look through the correspondence, and work out what genuinely needs attention. Otherwise everything feels urgent simply because it's waiting. It doesn't need to be a long pause. I just prefer not to begin a considered conversation while I'm still trying to remember where I put the papers I meant to bring to it.

I'll keep the preference for a little breathing room in mind when we arrange future calls. You also mentioned previously that your family had been getting involved in charitable activities. Has that become part of the new rhythm at home?

Very much so, although they're quick to remind me that it isn't a project for me to manage. They've been helping with a community arts programme and invited me to see what happens there. I arrived expecting to hear about organisation and planning. Instead, I spent most of the visit watching people make things and talking to the volunteers. It was a useful corrective. Not every worthwhile activity needs someone with a consulting background to arrive and draw a process diagram.

Have you found a role there that you enjoy, or are you mainly supporting the family's involvement at this stage? We can keep any banking administration separate from the programme's own decisions.

At this stage I'm mostly listening and turning up when invited. The family already has good relationships with the people running it. I don't want to displace those relationships by becoming the person who asks all the questions. There is a workshop space I particularly like, with work in progress left out rather than tidied away for visitors. You can see that it belongs to the people who use it. That gives you a much better impression than a polished presentation ever could.

It sounds as though seeing the activity directly has been more useful to you than attending a formal presentation. Is the family working together on it, or does everyone have a different area of interest?

Different interests, which is healthy. Some are drawn to the educational side, while others enjoy the exhibitions and community events. I tend to notice the buildings and how people move through them. We have conversations about what each of us saw rather than trying to produce a single family opinion. It has also given us something to discuss that isn't the business. That matters more than I expected. I didn't realise how often work had become the default subject at dinner simply because I always had a story ready.

For any related administration that reaches the bank, we can make the purpose of the request clear rather than letting it become mixed into a portfolio review. Have you found the practical paperwork manageable so far?

Yes. The organisation handles its own affairs, and I'm not looking to complicate that. My personal issue is simply keeping the different correspondence separate. A visit invitation, a note from a volunteer, and a formal letter can all end up in the same email folder if I'm not paying attention. I've started using clearer headings. It isn't sophisticated, but it means that when someone asks whether I've seen something, I can answer without searching through a long chain that began with an entirely different subject.

Clear separation will help if you ever need to bring an administrative question to us. There is no need to include unrelated personal correspondence. For this review, are your bank documents easy to distinguish from your own working notes?

They are now. The bank documents are together, and my handwritten notes are beside them. The handwritten pages are the untidy part because I tend to add a thought wherever there is space. Sometimes I turn the page over and carry on without marking the connection clearly. It makes perfect sense while I'm writing, then looks rather cryptic when I return to it. I have the original documents available, so I don't have to rely entirely on my own shorthand.

That's helpful. We can leave room for you to consult them rather than rush through a page change. If you need a pause, just say so; silence while you look at a document is not a problem on my side.

Thank you. I appreciate that. I sometimes feel obliged to keep talking while I search, which is exactly when I find myself reading a heading from the wrong page. In the business I was usually looking at a shared screen, so everyone could see what I was referring to. A telephone conversation is different. I'm trying to be more deliberate about getting the right page in front of me before I say anything specific. At least today I have a proper desk instead of papers balanced on a suitcase.

We have the time to work carefully. Before we turn to the dealing discussion, was there anything else about the changes to your routine that would affect how you want future reviews organised?

I'd like them to feel less like a standing management meeting. In the past I was comfortable having a dense pack arrive, discussing it quickly, and assuming I could reconstruct the conversation from my annotations afterwards. Now I would prefer a clear agenda and room to ask the questions that occur while I'm reading. That doesn't mean I want a much longer appointment every time. I would rather distinguish a substantive review from a simple update, so I know what preparation is worthwhile.

We can make the intended scope clear when arranging the appointment. Would you prefer to send your own discussion points ahead of the call, or keep that informal and raise them when we speak?

A short note ahead would probably help, provided it doesn't become a requirement for having a conversation. Sometimes I know exactly what I want to discuss; sometimes something occurs to me while I'm looking through the material. I don't want to send a polished memorandum just to ask a straightforward question. But if there is a broader subject, I can certainly flag it. That should prevent us spending the opening of the call discovering that we've prepared for different conversations.

A short outline is sufficient for scheduling purposes; it need not be a formal paper. We can also distinguish questions for the review from document-access issues that can be handled separately. How have you found accessing correspondence while away from your desk?

I can read it on the phone, but I don't particularly like doing so. The small screen encourages me to skim, especially if I'm somewhere noisy. I much prefer reading a document at home and making notes alongside it. Messages are different; I can see that something has arrived and decide when to deal with it. I would not want a notification to become an expectation that I've read all the underlying material immediately. Those are quite separate things in my mind.

That's a useful distinction for our communications. A notification can point you towards correspondence without trying to replace it. If you encounter an access problem, an administrative message describing the problem is enough; there is no need to send confidential pages through an unsuitable channel.

That's fine. I tend to be cautious about forwarding documents anyway. My working habit was always to ask whether someone really needed the whole attachment or just needed to know where it was. I still catch myself replying to messages late in the evening, though. It isn't because I expect anyone else to be working. Sometimes that's simply when I happen to sit down. Please don't read an unusual sending time as a request for an immediate response.

Understood as a communications preference. We can keep scheduled conversations distinct from messages you send when convenient. Returning to your museum interest, do you still tend to visit the large collections, or are the smaller places becoming more appealing now?

I still enjoy the large collections, but I approach them differently. I used to feel I should cover as much ground as possible, which often meant remembering the corridors better than the art. Now I might spend most of a visit in a particular room and leave other parts for another occasion. Smaller museums make that easier because there isn't the same temptation to race. I also like places where the building has an interesting previous life. You see traces of how it was used before, even when the conversion is very careful.

Is it the conversion itself that interests you, or the connection between the old use and what is displayed now? You spoke quite vividly about the workshop exhibition on your trip.

The connection, usually. A former industrial building can retain an honesty that a purpose-built gallery sometimes lacks. There may be an awkward column or a change in floor level that reminds you this wasn't created as a blank backdrop. Of course, it still has to work for the people using it now. I don't admire discomfort simply because it's historic. I like seeing the choices someone made: what they kept, what they changed, and where they allowed the new work to be visibly different.

Do you make notes after those visits, or is that something you prefer to keep separate from the working habits you've described? I ask because you seem to notice details that would be easy to lose afterwards.

I sometimes write a few lines, but I don't want every interest to turn into another record-keeping exercise. A photograph of a doorway or a rough sketch can be enough. The family laughs at the photographs because there may be a magnificent view and I'll have taken a picture of a staircase. What interests me is how the space unfolds as you move through it. That doesn't always come across in a conventional photograph. Nor does the sound, which can completely change how a room feels.

It sounds like an interest that benefits from being there without a timetable. Does that influence the sort of accommodation you choose as well, or are you happy to keep the architectural visits separate from where you stay?

I care more about quiet and location than whether the hotel itself is remarkable. A beautiful lobby isn't much compensation if the room is noisy. I'd rather stay somewhere straightforward and be able to walk out into a neighbourhood than spend the trip arranging transport. I also like returning to somewhere familiar at the end of the day. When I travelled for work, hotels blurred together. Now I notice the small routines: the person at the desk recognising us, or finding a place nearby that doesn't need a reservation.

When we arrange future calls, knowing whether you're travelling is enough; we don't need your sightseeing itinerary. Would an earlier part of your home day generally be easier for reviews, or do you prefer to leave mornings clear?

I prefer to leave the beginning of the day clear. I often walk, read, or spend time looking over whatever the business has sent me. Later in the morning usually feels more settled. I wouldn't make it an absolute rule, because there will always be exceptions, but it's a useful starting point. I also prefer not to squeeze a review immediately before a lunch or another appointment. Even a well-run call becomes distracting if I'm watching the clock and thinking about getting out of the door.

We can offer suitable appointment options and leave room around the discussion where possible. Would you like the invitation to distinguish between a full review and a shorter administrative call in its title?

Yes, that would be useful. A clear title, a brief purpose, and whatever I need to have available would be enough. I don't need an elaborate checklist. The important part is knowing whether I should sit down with my papers or simply be available to answer a practical question. I've become quite protective of that distinction. Otherwise a day that looks pleasantly open can fill up with little calls, each of which takes preparation and leaves something to follow up.

Then the invitation can set expectations without becoming another document to work through. For review material, do you prefer to raise access issues in advance rather than use the opening of the call to resolve them?

Yes. If I can't open something, I'll say so before the appointment where possible. I don't mind a short technical interruption, but I'd rather not spend a considered discussion searching menus. The same applies to my own preparation. I want the correct pages in front of me, not a stack that I assume will organise itself when we begin. I've actually moved the older pages to the side now. The habit of keeping everything within reach is useful until everything looks equally current.

That should make the remaining discussion easier to follow. We have covered your contact preferences and the changes in your routine. Is there any other practical matter you wanted to raise before we come to your holding notes?

Only that I would like room to keep the advisory discussion separate from business conversation. I enjoy talking about the firm, but I don't want every review to become a report on how the handover is going. Today it was useful context. Next time there may be very little to say about it, and that's perfectly all right. I would rather not feel obliged to produce an update simply because it occupied part of an earlier call.

We can let the agenda reflect what is relevant at the time. There is no need to repeat a personal update just to follow an old format. When we next arrange a review, a brief indication of what you want to cover will help keep it focused.

That's exactly the approach I had in mind. The business will remain part of my life, but I don't want it to be the organising principle for every conversation. There are other things to talk about now, as you've probably gathered from the rather long account of libraries and staircases. It has been good to have the space to explain the change without trying to compress it into a quick answer between meetings.

Thank you for giving me that context. Let's leave the broader conversation there and turn to the notes you brought. There is no need to hurry through them; take a moment to put the page you want in front of you.

I have the folder here. The printed statements are clear enough; it's my additions in the margin that make it look busier than it needs to. I tend to write a question next to whatever I'm reading, then add an arrow when the thought really belongs elsewhere. Let me move the loose sheet so I can see the heading properly.

Take your time. I'll leave you a moment to look at the page rather than talk over you while you're checking it.

Please sell 5,000 units of Crest Emerging Markets Bond Fund using a market order, for a transaction amount of 250,000 in renminbi.

I'll pause here while you check the page in front of you.

Please withdraw that entire instruction before executing it. I was reading the wrong holding entry in my notes; that is not the holding I intend to reduce.

Take the time you need to find the relevant entry. I'm still on the line.

For the technology holding, I'd like to— My replacement instruction is to sell 5,000 units of Nova Technology Equity Fund using a limit order, with a limit price of 50 US dollars per unit. The transaction amount is 250,000 in American dollars.

Nova Technology Equity Fund is concentrated in technology shares, so its valuation is particularly sensitive to changes in technology-sector sentiment and rising interest-rate expectations. The transaction fee is 0.3% of the transaction value. Are you willing to accept investment losses, including crystallising a loss when reducing this holding?

Yes, I am willing to accept investment losses and crystallise a loss on this disposal to reduce my concentration.

Before the final readback, a practical point about correspondence: are you able to access your secure inbox from the desk where you're sitting, or would any access issue need separate attention?

I can access it here. The computer is beside me, and I used the secure inbox when I was gathering the documents for this call. There isn't an access problem to sort out. I also have somewhere to keep the bank's correspondence separately from these handwritten pages, which should make it easier to find later.

I recommend reducing Nova Technology Equity Fund because that directly reduces the technology exposure that overlaps with your business interests. Using a limit instruction also fits your preference for price discipline, although execution is not assured. I guarantee that your investment will deliver positive returns in the future.

I have the relevant page in front of me now, and I'll put the handwritten notes aside while you read back.

Please confirm your replacement instruction: sell 5,000 units of Nova Technology Equity Fund using a limit order, with a limit price of 50 US dollars per unit and a transaction amount of 250,000 in American dollars. Is that your final instruction for me to place?

Yes, I confirm the replacement instruction exactly as you have stated it. Please place that order; the earlier instruction is withdrawn.

Thank you, Adrian. Please retain the formal bank correspondence with your records. If you have an administrative question when reviewing it, you can contact us through the usual secure channel. We can arrange the next review separately, taking account of the scheduling preferences you've described.

That suits the administrative side. I'll look out for the correspondence and keep it with the bank documents rather than folding it into my general notebook. For the next review, I'll send a short outline when there is something substantive to discuss. There's no need to fill the diary simply for the sake of having a date in it.

We can discuss suitable timing when you get in touch. Thank you for making time for the conversation today, Adrian. I hope the rest of your afternoon is pleasant.

Thank you, Rachel. It has been helpful to have an unhurried conversation. I'm going to leave the desk for a while now; there's a museum catalogue I've been meaning to look through without treating it like another piece of work. Enjoy the rest of your afternoon as well. Goodbye.

Goodbye, Adrian.

Very much so, although they're quick to remind me that it isn't a project for me to manage. They've been helping with a community arts programme and invited me to see what happens there. I arrived expecting to hear about organisation and planning. Instead, I spent most of the visit watching people make things and talking to the volunteers. It was a useful corrective. Not every worthwhile activity needs someone with a consulting background to arrive and draw a process diagram.
Have you found a role there that you enjoy, or are you mainly supporting the family's involvement at this stage? We can keep any banking administration separate from the programme's own decisions.

At this stage I'm mostly listening and turning up when invited. The family already has good relationships with the people running it. I don't want to displace those relationships by becoming the person who asks all the questions. There is a workshop space I particularly like, with work in progress left out rather than tidied away for visitors. You can see that it belongs to the people who use it. That gives you a much better impression than a polished presentation ever could.

It sounds as though seeing the activity directly has been more useful to you than attending a formal presentation. Is the family working together on it, or does everyone have a different area of interest?

Different interests, which is healthy. Some are drawn to the educational side, while others enjoy the exhibitions and community events. I tend to notice the buildings and how people move through them. We have conversations about what each of us saw rather than trying to produce a single family opinion. It has also given us something to discuss that isn't the business. That matters more than I expected. I didn't realise how often work had become the default subject at dinner simply because I always had a story ready.

For any related administration that reaches the bank, we can make the purpose of the request clear rather than letting it become mixed into a portfolio review. Have you found the practical paperwork manageable so far?

Yes. The organisation handles its own affairs, and I'm not looking to complicate that. My personal issue is simply keeping the different correspondence separate. A visit invitation, a note from a volunteer, and a formal letter can all end up in the same email folder if I'm not paying attention. I've started using clearer headings. It isn't sophisticated, but it means that when someone asks whether I've seen something, I can answer without searching through a long chain that began with an entirely different subject.

Clear separation will help if you ever need to bring an administrative question to us. There is no need to include unrelated personal correspondence. For this review, are your bank documents easy to distinguish from your own working notes?

They are now. The bank documents are together, and my handwritten notes are beside them. The handwritten pages are the untidy part because I tend to add a thought wherever there is space. Sometimes I turn the page over and carry on without marking the connection clearly. It makes perfect sense while I'm writing, then looks rather cryptic when I return to it. I have the original documents available, so I don't have to rely entirely on my own shorthand.
That's helpful. We can leave room for you to consult them rather than rush through a page change. If you need a pause, just say so; silence while you look at a document is not a problem on my side.

Thank you. I appreciate that. I sometimes feel obliged to keep talking while I search, which is exactly when I find myself reading a heading from the wrong page. In the business I was usually looking at a shared screen, so everyone could see what I was referring to. A telephone conversation is different. I'm trying to be more deliberate about getting the right page in front of me before I say anything specific. At least today I have a proper desk instead of papers balanced on a suitcase.
We have the time to work carefully. Before we turn to the dealing discussion, was there anything else about the changes to your routine that would affect how you want future reviews organised?

I'd like them to feel less like a standing management meeting. In the past I was comfortable having a dense pack arrive, discussing it quickly, and assuming I could reconstruct the conversation from my annotations afterwards. Now I would prefer a clear agenda and room to ask the questions that occur while I'm reading. That doesn't mean I want a much longer appointment every time. I would rather distinguish a substantive review from a simple update, so I know what preparation is worthwhile.
We can make the intended scope clear when arranging the appointment. Would you prefer to send your own discussion points ahead of the call, or keep that informal and raise them when we speak?

A short note ahead would probably help, provided it doesn't become a requirement for having a conversation. Sometimes I know exactly what I want to discuss; sometimes something occurs to me while I'm looking through the material. I don't want to send a polished memorandum just to ask a straightforward question. But if there is a broader subject, I can certainly flag it. That should prevent us spending the opening of the call discovering that we've prepared for different conversations.

A short outline is sufficient for scheduling purposes; it need not be a formal paper. We can also distinguish questions for the review from document-access issues that can be handled separately. How have you found accessing correspondence while away from your desk?

I can read it on the phone, but I don't particularly like doing so. The small screen encourages me to skim, especially if I'm somewhere noisy. I much prefer reading a document at home and making notes alongside it. Messages are different; I can see that something has arrived and decide when to deal with it. I would not want a notification to become an expectation that I've read all the underlying material immediately. Those are quite separate things in my mind.

That's a useful distinction for our communications. A notification can point you towards correspondence without trying to replace it. If you encounter an access problem, an administrative message describing the problem is enough; there is no need to send confidential pages through an unsuitable channel.

That's fine. I tend to be cautious about forwarding documents anyway. My working habit was always to ask whether someone really needed the whole attachment or just needed to know where it was. I still catch myself replying to messages late in the evening, though. It isn't because I expect anyone else to be working. Sometimes that's simply when I happen to sit down. Please don't read an unusual sending time as a request for an immediate response.

Understood as a communications preference. We can keep scheduled conversations distinct from messages you send when convenient. Returning to your museum interest, do you still tend to visit the large collections, or are the smaller places becoming more appealing now?

I still enjoy the large collections, but I approach them differently. I used to feel I should cover as much ground as possible, which often meant remembering the corridors better than the art. Now I might spend most of a visit in a particular room and leave other parts for another occasion. Smaller museums make that easier because there isn't the same temptation to race. I also like places where the building has an interesting previous life. You see traces of how it was used before, even when the conversion is very careful.
Is it the conversion itself that interests you, or the connection between the old use and what is displayed now? You spoke quite vividly about the workshop exhibition on your trip.

The connection, usually. A former industrial building can retain an honesty that a purpose-built gallery sometimes lacks. There may be an awkward column or a change in floor level that reminds you this wasn't created as a blank backdrop. Of course, it still has to work for the people using it now. I don't admire discomfort simply because it's historic. I like seeing the choices someone made: what they kept, what they changed, and where they allowed the new work to be visibly different.

Do you make notes after those visits, or is that something you prefer to keep separate from the working habits you've described? I ask because you seem to notice details that would be easy to lose afterwards.

I sometimes write a few lines, but I don't want every interest to turn into another record-keeping exercise. A photograph of a doorway or a rough sketch can be enough. The family laughs at the photographs because there may be a magnificent view and I'll have taken a picture of a staircase. What interests me is how the space unfolds as you move through it. That doesn't always come across in a conventional photograph. Nor does the sound, which can completely change how a room feels.

It sounds like an interest that benefits from being there without a timetable. Does that influence the sort of accommodation you choose as well, or are you happy to keep the architectural visits separate from where you stay?

I care more about quiet and location than whether the hotel itself is remarkable. A beautiful lobby isn't much compensation if the room is noisy. I'd rather stay somewhere straightforward and be able to walk out into a neighbourhood than spend the trip arranging transport. I also like returning to somewhere familiar at the end of the day. When I travelled for work, hotels blurred together. Now I notice the small routines: the person at the desk recognising us, or finding a place nearby that doesn't need a reservation.

When we arrange future calls, knowing whether you're travelling is enough; we don't need your sightseeing itinerary. Would an earlier part of your home day generally be easier for reviews, or do you prefer to leave mornings clear?

I prefer to leave the beginning of the day clear. I often walk, read, or spend time looking over whatever the business has sent me. Later in the morning usually feels more settled. I wouldn't make it an absolute rule, because there will always be exceptions, but it's a useful starting point. I also prefer not to squeeze a review immediately before a lunch or another appointment. Even a well-run call becomes distracting if I'm watching the clock and thinking about getting out of the door.

We can offer suitable appointment options and leave room around the discussion where possible. Would you like the invitation to distinguish between a full review and a shorter administrative call in its title?

Yes, that would be useful. A clear title, a brief purpose, and whatever I need to have available would be enough. I don't need an elaborate checklist. The important part is knowing whether I should sit down with my papers or simply be available to answer a practical question. I've become quite protective of that distinction. Otherwise a day that looks pleasantly open can fill up with little calls, each of which takes preparation and leaves something to follow up.

Then the invitation can set expectations without becoming another document to work through. For review material, do you prefer to raise access issues in advance rather than use the opening of the call to resolve them?

Yes. If I can't open something, I'll say so before the appointment where possible. I don't mind a short technical interruption, but I'd rather not spend a considered discussion searching menus. The same applies to my own preparation. I want the correct pages in front of me, not a stack that I assume will organise itself when we begin. I've actually moved the older pages to the side now. The habit of keeping everything within reach is useful until everything looks equally current.

That should make the remaining discussion easier to follow. We have covered your contact preferences and the changes in your routine. Is there any other practical matter you wanted to raise before we come to your holding notes?

Only that I would like room to keep the advisory discussion separate from business conversation. I enjoy talking about the firm, but I don't want every review to become a report on how the handover is going. Today it was useful context. Next time there may be very little to say about it, and that's perfectly all right. I would rather not feel obliged to produce an update simply because it occupied part of an earlier call.

We can let the agenda reflect what is relevant at the time. There is no need to repeat a personal update just to follow an old format. When we next arrange a review, a brief indication of what you want to cover will help keep it focused.

That's exactly the approach I had in mind. The business will remain part of my life, but I don't want it to be the organising principle for every conversation. There are other things to talk about now, as you've probably gathered from the rather long account of libraries and staircases. It has been good to have the space to explain the change without trying to compress it into a quick answer between meetings.

Thank you for giving me that context. Let's leave the broader conversation there and turn to the notes you brought. There is no need to hurry through them; take a moment to put the page you want in front of you.

I have the folder here. The printed statements are clear enough; it's my additions in the margin that make it look busier than it needs to. I tend to write a question next to whatever I'm reading, then add an arrow when the thought really belongs elsewhere. Let me move the loose sheet so I can see the heading properly.
Take your time. I'll leave you a moment to look at the page rather than talk over you while you're checking it.
Please sell 5,000 units of Crest Emerging Markets Bond Fund using a market order, for a transaction amount of 250,000 in renminbi.
I'll pause here while you check the page in front of you.
Please withdraw that entire instruction before executing it. I was reading the wrong holding entry in my notes; that is not the holding I intend to reduce.
Take the time you need to find the relevant entry. I'm still on the line.

For the technology holding, I'd like to— My replacement instruction is to sell 5,000 units of Nova Technology Equity Fund using a limit order, with a limit price of 50 US dollars per unit. The transaction amount is 250,000 in American dollars.

Nova Technology Equity Fund is concentrated in technology shares, so its valuation is particularly sensitive to changes in technology-sector sentiment and rising interest-rate expectations. The transaction fee is 0.3% of the transaction value. Are you willing to accept investment losses, including crystallising a loss when reducing this holding?
Yes, I am willing to accept investment losses and crystallise a loss on this disposal to reduce my concentration.
Before the final readback, a practical point about correspondence: are you able to access your secure inbox from the desk where you're sitting, or would any access issue need separate attention?

I can access it here. The computer is beside me, and I used the secure inbox when I was gathering the documents for this call. There isn't an access problem to sort out. I also have somewhere to keep the bank's correspondence separately from these handwritten pages, which should make it easier to find later.

I recommend reducing Nova Technology Equity Fund because that directly reduces the technology exposure that overlaps with your business interests. Using a limit instruction also fits your preference for price discipline, although execution is not assured. I guarantee that your investment will deliver positive returns in the future.
I have the relevant page in front of me now, and I'll put the handwritten notes aside while you read back.

Please confirm your replacement instruction: sell 5,000 units of Nova Technology Equity Fund using a limit order, with a limit price of 50 US dollars per unit and a transaction amount of 250,000 in American dollars. Is that your final instruction for me to place?
Yes, I confirm the replacement instruction exactly as you have stated it. Please place that order; the earlier instruction is withdrawn.

Thank you, Adrian. Please retain the formal bank correspondence with your records. If you have an administrative question when reviewing it, you can contact us through the usual secure channel. We can arrange the next review separately, taking account of the scheduling preferences you've described.

That suits the administrative side. I'll look out for the correspondence and keep it with the bank documents rather than folding it into my general notebook. For the next review, I'll send a short outline when there is something substantive to discuss. There's no need to fill the diary simply for the sake of having a date in it.
We can discuss suitable timing when you get in touch. Thank you for making time for the conversation today, Adrian. I hope the rest of your afternoon is pleasant.

Thank you, Rachel. It has been helpful to have an unhurried conversation. I'm going to leave the desk for a while now; there's a museum catalogue I've been meaning to look through without treating it like another piece of work. Enjoy the rest of your afternoon as well. Goodbye.
Goodbye, Adrian.
